title: Setup, turn, punchline
goal: Follow and retell a fıkra, and recognize its tense and its punchline.

intro.text: A *fıkra* is a joke told as a story: a short setup, a turn, and a one-line punchline. Nasreddin Hoca's are told in `-mIş`, like tales; modern jokes are often told in the present and open with *Adamın biri…*

vocab.en: joke, funny anecdote; also a newspaper column
witticism, joke; the point of a joke (espri yapmak: to make a joke)
a lame joke, a joke that falls flat
a certain man, a man (opening a joke)
yeast; yogurt starter (maya çalmak: to add starter to milk)
to attempt the impossible (literally, to put starter in a lake)
But what if it works! (literally, what if it takes)

exercises.title: Kazan doğurdu
exercises.passage:
Nasreddin Hoca bir gün komşusundan büyük bir kazan ödünç almış. Ertesi gün kazanı geri götürmüş, ama içine küçük bir tencere koymuş. Komşu şaşırmış: “Bu tencere ne?” Hoca gülümsemiş: “Kazanınız doğurdu, bu da yavrusu.” Komşu hiç itiraz etmemiş, tencereyi de almış.

Bir hafta sonra Hoca kazanı yine istemiş. Komşu seve seve vermiş. Ama bu kez günler geçmiş, kazan geri gelmemiş. Sonunda komşu Hoca'nın kapısını çalmış: “Hocam, kazanım nerede?” Hoca üzgün üzgün başını sallamış: “Başınız sağ olsun, kazanınız öldü.”

Komşu bağırmış: “Hiç kazan ölür mü?” Hoca da sakin sakin cevap vermiş: “Doğurduğuna inandın da öldüğüne neden inanmıyorsun?”
exercises.translation: One day Nasreddin Hoca borrowed a big cauldron from his neighbour. The next day he took it back, but he had put a small pot inside it. The neighbour was surprised: 'What's this pot?' The Hoca smiled: 'Your cauldron has given birth, and this is its baby.' The neighbour didn't object at all, and took the pot too. A week later the Hoca asked for the cauldron again, and the neighbour gladly gave it. But this time days went by and the cauldron didn't come back. In the end the neighbour knocked on the Hoca's door: 'Hoca, where is my cauldron?' The Hoca sadly shook his head: 'My condolences: your cauldron has died.' The neighbour shouted: 'Since when do cauldrons die?' And the Hoca calmly replied: 'You believed it gave birth, so why won't you believe it died?'

questions.q: What did the Hoca bring back the first time?
options: The cauldron, with a small pot inside

questions.q: What does the Hoca's last line turn against the neighbour?
options: His own acceptance of the first absurd claim
questions.explain: The neighbour happily accepted that a cauldron can give birth, because it gained him a pot. The punchline holds him to his own logic.

questions.q: Why is the story told in `-mIş`?
options: It is a traditional story the teller didn't witness
Because `-DI` can't be used for long ago
questions.explain: Fıkras, like tales, come down by hearsay: *almış, götürmüş, demiş*.

questions.q: What is funny about *Başınız sağ olsun*?
options: It is the condolence formula, said about a pot
It is rude to the neighbour
It shows the Hoca is really sad
questions.explain: *Başınız sağ olsun* is said to someone who has lost a relative ([A2 unit 7](gp-set-wishes)); for a cauldron it plays the absurd premise to the end.

exercises.en: You believed it gave birth, so why won't you believe it died?

reject.why: The neighbour refuses now, as they speak: the present continuous, *inanmıyorsun*.

exercises.hint: The first verb is about what he did; the second about what he refuses now.
exercises.explain: *İnanmak* takes the dative: *doğurduğuna*, *öldüğüne*. *Da* links the two as **and yet**.

accept: Eat up, my [fur coat|coat|fur], eat up!
Eat, my dear fur coat, eat!
exercises.explain: The Hoca's line to his coat, which was honoured at the feast instead of him. Today it is said of people judged by their clothes.

exercises.question: A friend says: *Bu projeyle şirketi kurtaracağını mı sanıyorsun? Göle maya çalıyorsun.* What does she mean?
options: Your plan will take time, but it will work
You are spending too much on food

why.1: The idiom says the opposite: the starter will never turn a lake into yogurt.
why.2: The words are literal only in the Hoca's story.
why.3: Nothing in the sentence is about food.

exercises.explain: *Göle maya çalmak*: to attempt the impossible, after the fıkra of the Hoca and the lake. The Hoca's reply, *Ya tutarsa!*, is the hopeful answer.

exercises.prompt: A man walked into a corner shop. (Start the joke the Turkish way.)

reject.why: Correct Turkish, but jokes open with *Adamın biri*: try that.

exercises.explain: *Adamın biri*, literally 'one of the man', is the classic opening. `-mIş` is the traditional tense; the present (*giriyor*) is common in modern jokes.

exercises.question: A friend starts a modern joke and wants it to feel like a scene happening in front of you. Which opening fits?

why.1: `-mIştIr` belongs to encyclopedias and confident guesses ([C1 unit 2](gp-dir-assumption)).
why.2: `-mAktA` is formal written Turkish ([B2 unit 5](gp-makta)), the opposite of a joke's tone.
why.3: The future announces a plan; it doesn't tell a story.

exercises.explain: Jokes are often told in the present continuous or the aorist, like a scene played out before you; traditional fıkras keep `-mIş`.

exercises.task: Retell the cauldron story in four or five sentences of Turkish, in `-mIş`, and end with the Hoca's punchline as direct speech.
models: Nasreddin Hoca bir gün komşusundan bir kazan ödünç almış. Ertesi gün kazanın içine küçük bir tencere koyup geri vermiş: “Kazanınız doğurdu.” demiş. Bir süre sonra kazanı yine almış, ama bu kez geri getirmemiş: “Kazanınız öldü.” Komşu “Kazan ölür mü?” diye sorunca Hoca şöyle demiş: “Doğurduğuna inandın da öldüğüne neden inanmıyorsun?”
checklist: Setup: who borrowed what from whom
The turn in two steps: the small pot, then the cauldron that never comes back
The punchline as direct speech, with *inanmak* and the dative

exercises.explain: *Espriyi anlamak* is **to get the joke**; with a joke told as a story, *Fıkrayı anladın mı?* works too.

exercises.question: A colleague's pun is met with total silence, and someone says *Çok soğuk bir espriydi.* What happened?

why.1: *Soğuk* here is figurative: a cold joke leaves the room cold.
why.2: A rude joke would be *kaba*, not *soğuk*.

exercises.explain: A *soğuk espri* is a lame joke, one that falls flat; TDK records the compound.
